karten.r: A small rectangular battery is labeled 9 V. This figure is a voltage.
An electric field determines, for every location, what force acts on a charge there.
The potential determines, for every location, how much energy per coulomb a charge has there relative to a freely chosen zero point, the reference point.
The discipline of electrical engineering is the engineering science that moves electric charges in a controlled way in order to transmit energy and process information.

karten.v: What does “atom, protons, neutrons, electrons” mean?
karten.r: An atom has a tiny nucleus of protons and neutrons, around which electrons move (Fig. 1).
An atom contains as many protons as electrons; seen from outside, their charges cancel, and it is neutral.
An atom with a surplus charge is called an ion.
Someone coming in from the snow calls a room warm; someone coming out of the sauna calls it cool. Such judgments are qualitative.
A thermometer shows both of them 21 °C; that is quantitative: a number on a scale, independent of who is measuring.
A physical quantity is a measurable property, the product of numerical value and unit.
An electric current is moving charge; one ampere transports one coulomb per second.
SI prefixes scale a numerical value by powers of ten.
A force deforms a body that is held in place or accelerates a movable one.
Energy is the capacity to do work.
Force and displacement are vectors: quantities with magnitude and direction, written with an arrow, $\vec F$.

Velocity is the change of position per time, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{d} s/\mathrm{d} t}$, acceleration the change of velocity per time, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{a}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{d} v/\mathrm{d} t}$.
A body with the velocity $v$ carries the kinetic energy $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W_\mathrm{kin}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12m\,v^2}$.

$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{[F]}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm N}$; at the surface of the Earth, about 1 N acts on 100 g. $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\gamma}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{6.674\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}}$ is the gravitational constant.
The product $\vec F\cdot\Delta\vec s$ is called the scalar product; its result is a number.
The integral is called a line integral: the path is divided into short straight pieces and their contributions are summed.
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\text{quantity}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\text{numerical value}\cdot\text{unit}.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 1.2 (Force and work)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{F}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{m\,a,\qquad F}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\gamma\,\frac{m\,M}{r^2}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\Delta W}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\vec F\cdot\Delta\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{F\,\Delta s\cos\alpha,\qquad W}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{P_1}^{P_2}\vec F\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 1.3 (Constant acceleration and kinetic energy)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{v_0+a\,t,\qquad s(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{s_0+v_0\,t+\tfrac12a\,t^2.}$$

karten.z:
With the initial values $s_0$ and $v_0$ at $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, for constant $a$

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{v_0+a\,t,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{s_0+v_0\,t+\tfrac12a\,t^2.}$$
(1.4)

A body with the velocity $v$ carries the kinetic energy $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W_\mathrm{kin}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12m\,v^2}$.
karten.s0: From (1.4) with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v_0}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s_0}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$ it follows that $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{v/a}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12a\,t^2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{v^2/(2a)}$.
s: Over this distance, a constant force $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{F}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{m\,a}$ does the work $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{F\,s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{m\,a\,v^2/(2a)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12m\,v^2}$.

karten.v: What does “electron deficit, electron excess” mean?
karten.r: A body with an electron deficit is positively charged, one with an electron excess negatively.
The elementary charge $e$ is the smallest charge occurring freely.
In a closed system, the sum of all charges stays constant (conservation of charge).
In a conductor such as metal, at least one electron per atom can wander through the entire body.
In an insulator such as glass or rubber, the electrons stay with their atoms.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Q}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(N_\mathrm{p}-N_\mathrm{e})\,e,\qquad e}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1.602\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C},\qquad[Q]}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm C}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{A\,s}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Why rubbing does not change the total charge” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Q}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(N_\mathrm{p}-N_\mathrm{e})\,e,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{e}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1.602\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{[Q]}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm C}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{A\,s}.}$$
(2.1)
karten.s0: Two bodies together carry $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Q_1+Q_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\bigl[(N_\mathrm{p1}+N_\mathrm{p2})-(N_\mathrm{e1}+N_\mathrm{e2})\bigr]e}$.
s: If an electron passes from 1 to 2, $N_\mathrm{e1}$ decreases by one and $N_\mathrm{e2}$ increases by one; the bracket stays the same.
The charges “generated” by rubbing always add up to zero.

karten.r: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varepsilon_0}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{8.854\cdot10^{-12}}$ A s/(V m) is called the electric constant.
The bodies must be small compared with $r$ (point charges) and at rest.
Several charges act independently, and their forces add as vectors (superposition).

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{F}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,\frac{|Q_\mathrm{A}\,Q_\mathrm{B}|}{r^2},\qquad k}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{8.99\cdot10^{9}\,\frac{\mathrm{N\,m^2}}{\mathrm{C^2}}}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\vec F_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,\frac{Q_\mathrm{A}\,Q_\mathrm{B}}{r^2}\cdot\frac{\vec r}{r}.}$$

karten.v: How can “From experiment to law” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{F}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,\frac{|Q_\mathrm{A}\,Q_\mathrm{B}|}{r^2},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{k}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{8.99\cdot10^{9}\,\frac{\mathrm{N\,m^2}}{\mathrm{C^2}}}$$
(3.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\vec F_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,\frac{Q_\mathrm{A}\,Q_\mathrm{B}}{r^2}\cdot\frac{\vec r}{r}.}$$
(3.2)
karten.s0: The law is a measurement result.
s: Individually, the series of experiments give $F\sim Q_\mathrm{A}$, $F\sim Q_\mathrm{B}$, $F\sim1/r^2$ and $\vec F\parallel\vec r$, together $F\sim Q_\mathrm{A}Q_\mathrm{B}/r^2$, and the factor is $k$.

If one assumes $F\sim1/r^{2\pm\delta}$, the limit on $\delta$ fell from 0.02 with Cavendish (18th century) via $5\cdot10^{-5}$ with Maxwell (19th century) to $10^{-13}$ (Bartlett and others, 1970) and $3\cdot10^{-16}$ (Williams and others, 1971).

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 4.1 (Electric field strength)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\vec E:=\lim_{Q\to0}\frac{\vec F}{Q},\qquad\text{hence}\quad\vec F}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q\cdot\vec E.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 4.2 (Field of point charges)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\vec E}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,\frac{Q_0}{r^2}\cdot\frac{\vec r}{r},\qquad E}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,\frac{|Q_0|}{r^2},}$$

karten.v: the ______ on a charge is its charge times the field at its location.
karten.r: the force on a charge is its charge times the field at its location.

karten.v: How can “Field of a point charge” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\vec E}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,\frac{Q_0}{r^2}\cdot\frac{\vec r}{r},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{E}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,\frac{|Q_0|}{r^2},}$$
(4.2)
karten.s0: By (3.2), a test charge $Q$ experiences the force $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\vec F}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,Q\,Q_0/r^2\cdot\vec r/r}$.
s: Dividing by $Q$ removes $Q$; the result depends only on $Q_0$ and the location.
The sum rule follows from the superposition of forces.

karten.r: In metal, the free electrons move until no force acts on them any more. This displacement is called electrostatic induction.
A field line is a curve whose tangent at each point has the direction of $\vec E$; the density of the lines shows the strength of the field.
Field lines begin on positive charges (sources) and end on negative ones (sinks), never in empty space.
A charge-free cavity enclosed by the conductor is field-free (shielding).

karten.v: How can “Where the rules come from” be derived?
karten.z:
A field line is a curve whose tangent at each point has the direction of $\vec E$; the density of the lines shows the strength of the field. The following hold:

  1. Field lines begin on positive charges (sources) and end on negative ones (sinks), never in empty space. For a single charge, the other end runs off to infinity.

  2. Field lines do not cross.

  3. They are perpendicular to the surface of a conductor.

  4. Inside a conductor, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\vec E}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$. A charge-free cavity enclosed by the conductor is field-free (shielding).
karten.s0: ⁠Rule 2. At an intersection, $\vec E$ would have two directions, but the force on a test charge is unique.
s: ⁠Rule 4, metal. If there were a field in the metal, the free electrons would keep moving. Rest is reached only when the displaced charges exactly cancel the external field inside. Excess charges sit on the surface.
⁠Rule 3. A field component along the surface would push the electrons along it. At rest, only the perpendicular component remains.

⁠Rule 4, cavity. The external field ends on the induced charges of the outer side. With no charge in the cavity, a line there would have to run from wall to wall. A charge could gain energy along this line and return at no cost through the field-free metal. That would be energy from nothing, which Stage 6 rules out.

karten.r: Equivalently, the integral over any closed path is zero; the field is curl-free.
(6.2) requires charges at rest and no changing magnetic field (Stage 10). Such a field is called electrostatic.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 6.1 (Work in the electric field)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{P_1}^{P_2}\vec F\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q\int_{P_1}^{P_2}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s,\qquad\text{in a uniform field}\quad W_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q\,E\,s\cos\alpha.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\oint_L\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0.}$$

karten.v: How can “Why the work does not depend on the path” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{P_1}^{P_2}\vec F\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q\int_{P_1}^{P_2}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\text{in a uniform field}\quad W_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q\,E\,s\cos\alpha.}$$
(6.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\oint_L\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0.}$$
(6.2)
karten.s0:
⁠One point charge. Let $Q$ move in the field of $Q_0$ from $r_1$ to $r_2$. The path is split into pieces along the radius and across it. Across the radius, the field is perpendicular to the path, so only the change in distance counts:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q\int_{r_1}^{r_2}k\,\frac{Q_0}{r^2}\,\mathrm{d} r}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,Q\,Q_0\Bigl(\frac{1}{r_1}-\frac{1}{r_2}\Bigr).}$$
s: ⁠Arbitrary charges at rest. Every such field is a sum of point-charge fields, and the work is the sum of the individual works.

⁠Closed path. If path $a$ leads from $P_1$ to $P_2$ and path $b$ back, the return path read in the opposite direction changes sign: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\oint\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_a\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s-\int_{b,\,P_1\to P_2}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, because both paths give the same value.

karten.r: Locations of equal potential form equipotential surfaces.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi(P)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{P}^{P_0}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\int_{P_0}^{P}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s,\qquad[\varphi]}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{\mathrm J}{\mathrm C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm V.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 7.2 (Work as a potential difference, two profiles)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q\,\bigl(\varphi(P_1)-\varphi(P_2)\bigr).}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi(x)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varphi(0)-E\,x,\qquad\varphi(r)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,\frac{Q_0}{r}.}$$

karten.v: the ______ is the energy per charge at a location, measured from the reference point.
karten.r: the potential is the energy per charge at a location, measured from the reference point.

karten.v: How can “Work as a potential difference” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q\,\bigl(\varphi(P_1)-\varphi(P_2)\bigr).}$$
(7.2)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi(x)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varphi(0)-E\,x,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi(r)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,\frac{Q_0}{r}.}$$
(7.3)
karten.s0:
Because the work does not depend on the path, one may go from $P_1$ via $P_0$ to $P_2$:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\int_{P_1}^{P_2}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{P_1}^{P_0}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s+\int_{P_0}^{P_2}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varphi(P_1)-\varphi(P_2).}$$
s: Without path independence, $\varphi$ would not even be unique. The profiles (7.3) follow from (7.1) with constant $E$ and from the derivation in Stage 6 with $r_2\to\infty$.

karten.r: The point of a circuit that is assigned $\varphi:=0$ V is called ground or reference potential, written GND.

karten.v: What does “circuit diagrams, reference arrow” mean?
karten.r: In circuit diagrams, the drawings of a circuit, this is shown by a reference arrow from point 1 to point 2 (Fig. 9).

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 8.1 (Electric voltage and ground)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varphi(P_1)-\varphi(P_2)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{P_1}^{P_2}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{W_{12}}{Q},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varphi_2+U_{12}.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 8.2 (Uniform field, freedom of the reference point)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{E}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U}{d},\qquad\varphi'(P)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varphi(P)+c\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\varphi'_1-\varphi'_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_{12}.}$$

karten.v: ______ is energy per charge between two points.
karten.r: voltage is energy per charge between two points.

karten.v: How can “Pair of plates and reference point” be derived?
karten.s0: ⁠Field strength. Between A and B, $\vec E$ is constant and points along the path: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_0^dE\,\mathrm{d} x}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{E\,d}$.
s:
⁠Reference point. With (7.1) and path independence,

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi'(P)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{P}^{P_0'}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{P}^{P_0}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s+\int_{P_0}^{P_0'}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varphi(P)+c.}$$
The second integral does not depend on $P$, so it drops out of the difference.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 9.1 (Charge in the field)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tfrac12m\,v^2+Q\,\varphi}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\text{constant}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sqrt{\frac{2\,|Q\,U|}{m}},\qquad a}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{|Q|\,E}{m},\qquad t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{2\,d}{v}.}$$

karten.v: if a ______ in vacuum passes through a voltage, its kinetic energy changes by charge times voltage, regardless of path and distance.
karten.r: if a charge in vacuum passes through a voltage, its kinetic energy changes by charge times voltage, regardless of path and distance.

karten.v: How can “Energy theorem and flight time” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tfrac12m\,v^2+Q\,\varphi}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\text{constant}.}$$
(9.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sqrt{\frac{2\,|Q\,U|}{m}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{a}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{|Q|\,E}{m},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{2\,d}{v}.}$$
(9.2)
karten.s0: The work of the field becomes kinetic energy entirely: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac12mv_2^2-\frac12mv_1^2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{W_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)}$.
s: Rearranging gives (9.1).
With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$ it follows that $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{|Q\,U|}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12m\,v^2}$.
At constant acceleration the average speed is $v/2$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{d/(v/2)}$.

karten.r: In 1820 Ørsted saw a compass needle deflect next to a current-carrying wire: moving charge produces a magnetic field $H$.
In 1831 Faraday reversed the idea: a magnet that he moved in a coil, a wire wound into turns, produced a voltage at its ends.
In 1831 Faraday reversed the idea: a magnet that he moved in a coil, a wire wound into turns, produced a voltage at its ends. This is called induction.
In 1864 Maxwell combined everything into electromagnetism.
The mechanism of induction is a new field: a changing magnetic field produces an electric field with closed lines, a curl field.
The direction of the magnetic field is given by the right-hand rule: the thumb points in the conventional current direction, the fingers in the direction of the field.

The magnetic flux $\Phi$ measures how much magnetic field passes through the coil area, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{[\Phi]}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{V\,s}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{Wb}}$ (weber).
The flux density here is the measure of the density of the field lines.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 10.1 (Law of induction)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u_\mathrm{ind}(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-N\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d} t}.}$$
The node rule says that no current disappears at a junction.

The charge density $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{q}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\Delta Q/\Delta V}$ is the charge per volume.
The electric current (current for short) is the charge that passes through an area per time.
Second, the circuit must be closed, that is, a path that returns to itself.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 1.1 (Current and current density)”?

karten.v: How can “Current from density and velocity” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\begin{aligned} i&=\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}=\frac{\mathrm{d} Q}{\mathrm{d} t},\qquad I=q\,v\,A,\qquad [I]=\mathrm{C/s}=\mathrm A,\\ j&=\frac IA=q\,v,\qquad\vec j=q\,\vec v. \end{aligned}$$
(1.1)(1.2)

In this time, the electron covers on average the mean free path $\lambda$.

karten.v: How can “From field to drift” be derived?
karten.z:
If each flight between two collisions takes the time $T$, then

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{|\vec v_\mathrm{max}|}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{e\,|\vec E|}{m_\mathrm e}\,T,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\vec v_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\mu\,\vec E,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mu}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{e\,T}{2\,m_\mathrm e}.}$$
(2.1)

With Stage 1, the current gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{j/(n\,e)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I/(n\,e\,A)}$.

s: A flight starts with a directed part of zero, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{a\,t}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v_\mathrm{max}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{a\,T}$.
The sawtooth has the mean value $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v_\mathrm{max}/2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{e\,E\,T/(2\,m_\mathrm e)}$.

karten.r: $\sigma$ is the conductivity in S/m, $\rho$ the resistivity in $\Omega\,\mathrm m$.
$G$ is the conductance in S (siemens), $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{1\,\mathrm{S}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1\,\Omega^{-1}}$.
The conductor must be linear ($\vec j$ proportional to $\vec E$) and homogeneous (the same material everywhere).
The power, the energy per time, is therefore $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U\,I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,I^2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \vec j&=\sigma\,\vec E,\qquad\sigma=n\,e\,\mu,\qquad\rho=\frac1\sigma,\\ U&=R\,I,\qquad R=\frac{L}{\sigma\,A}=\rho\,\frac LA,\qquad G=\frac1R=\frac IU. \end{aligned}$$

karten.v: How can “From field to component” be derived?
karten.z:
For a conductor with the electron density $n$,

$$\begin{aligned} \vec j&=\sigma\,\vec E,\qquad\sigma=n\,e\,\mu,\qquad\rho=\frac1\sigma,\\ U&=R\,I,\qquad R=\frac{L}{\sigma\,A}=\rho\,\frac LA,\qquad G=\frac1R=\frac IU. \end{aligned}$$
(3.1)(3.2)
karten.s0:
Current density of the electrons, Stage 1, with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{q}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-n\,e}$ and (2.1):

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\vec j}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{q\,\vec v_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(-n\,e)(-\mu\,\vec E)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{n\,e\,\mu\,\vec E}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sigma\,\vec E.}$$
s:
The field is uniform, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{E\,L}$ (Chapter 1). Thus

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{j\,A}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sigma\,E\,A}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{\sigma\,A}{L}\,U\quad\Longrightarrow\quad U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{L}{\sigma\,A}\,I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,I.}$$

karten.v: What does “Metal-film or carbon-film resistors” mean?
karten.r: Metal-film or carbon-film resistors carry a thin layer on a ceramic body.
Wire-wound resistors withstand high power and temperature and are suited to small values.
SMD resistors (Surface Mounted Device) are soldered directly onto the circuit board.
An E series E$N$ contains $N$ values per decade; according to DIN IEC 60063 there are E3, E6, E12, E24, E48, E96 and E192.
The temperature coefficient $\alpha$ has the unit 1/K: copper $3.9\cdot10^{-3}$, tungsten $4.5\cdot10^{-3}$, carbon $-0.5\cdot10^{-3}$, constantan around $10^{-5}$.
For $\alpha>0$, the material is called PTC (positive temperature coefficient) or cold conductor: it conducts better when cold.
For $\alpha<0$, it is called NTC (negative temperature coefficient) or hot conductor.
Compensated alloys such as constantan: the collisions with the irregularly embedded impurity atoms predominate and hardly depend on temperature.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{w}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\bigl(\sqrt[N]{10}\,\bigr)^{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sqrt[N]{10^{i}},\qquad i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0,1,\dots,N-1.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R(\vartheta)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R(\vartheta_0)\,\bigl(1+\alpha_{\vartheta_0}\,(\vartheta-\vartheta_0)\bigr).}$$
A two-terminal element is a component that can be fully described by the current and voltage between its two terminals.
In the steady state (time-independent), that is its characteristic curve $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{f(U)}$.
A black box is a system whose outward behavior is known but whose construction is unknown or unimportant.
A network is an interconnection of two-terminal elements.
Such a linear two-terminal element is the ohmic resistor (Fig. 4 right, each straight line one value).
For a nonlinear two-terminal element such as the incandescent lamp (Fig. 5 right), $U/I$ depends on the operating point, and (5.1) does not hold there.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 5.1 (Two-terminal element, black box, network)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac IU}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\text{const}\quad\text{or}\quad R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac UI}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\text{const}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,I\quad\text{(PSC)},\qquad U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-R\,I\quad\text{(ASC)}.}$$
A node is a point at which the current branches.
A branch connects two nodes via two-terminal elements, and a current flows in it.
The graph is the representation made of nodes and branches.
A mesh is a closed path in which each node is connected to exactly two neighboring branches.
A tree is a connected subgraph that contains all nodes and forms no mesh.
The remaining branches are called link branches.
Meshes are called linearly independent if they can be ordered so that each contains at least one branch missing from the previous ones.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 6.2 (Number of independent meshes)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{m}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{z-k+1}$$

karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{m}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{z-k+1}$$
(6.1)
karten.s0: Build a tree: starting at one node, each new branch brings in exactly one new node; otherwise a mesh would arise.
s: For $k$ nodes you need $k-1$ tree branches.
That leaves $z-(k-1)$ link branches.
In the tree, there is exactly one path between two nodes, so each link branch closes exactly one mesh.
It contains no other link branch, which is why these meshes are independent.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 7.1 (Node rule, Kirchhoff's first law)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\sum_{\nu=1}^{N}I_\nu}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0\quad\text{(all arrows toward the node)},\qquad\sum I_\mathrm{in}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sum I_\mathrm{out}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Node rule from charge conservation” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\sum_{\nu=1}^{N}I_\nu}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0\quad\text{(all arrows toward the node)},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\sum I_\mathrm{in}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sum I_\mathrm{out}.}$$
(7.1)
karten.s0: For the charge $Q_\mathrm K$ on the node, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathrm{d} Q_\mathrm K/\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sum I_\nu}$, because charge neither arises nor disappears.
s: An estimate with Chapter 1 shows how small $Q_\mathrm K$ stays: a metal sphere with a radius of 1 cm has the potential $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k_\mathrm C\,Q/r}$ with the Coulomb constant $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{k_\mathrm C}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{8.99\cdot10^{9}\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}}$.
For 9 V, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Q}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{10}$ pC is enough.
A surplus of 3 mA supplies that in 3.3 ns.
That is why $\mathrm{d} Q_\mathrm K/\mathrm{d} t$ is negligible compared with the currents, and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\sum I_\nu}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$ remains.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 8.1 (Mesh rule, Kirchhoff's second law)”?
karten.r: $$ extcolor{#1b7f4a}{\sum_{ u=1}^{N}U_ u} extcolor{#15633a}{=} extcolor{#c2410c}{0,\qquad U_ u ext{ counted positive along the traversal, negative against it.}}$$

karten.v: How can “Mesh rule from the potential” be derived?
karten.z:
$$ extcolor{#1b7f4a}{\sum_{ u=1}^{N}U_ u} extcolor{#15633a}{=} extcolor{#c2410c}{0,}$$
$$U_ u ext{ counted positive along the traversal, negative against it.}$$
(8.1)
karten.s0:
By Chapter 1, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varphi_1-\varphi_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{P_1}^{P_2}\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}$ is independent of the path, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\oint\vec E\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$. $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)+(\varphi_2-\varphi_3)+\dots+(\varphi_N-\varphi_1)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0.}$$

karten.r: $R_\mathrm{tot}$ is the total resistance, the one resistor that replaces the chain.
The divider rule holds only when unloaded: no current may be drawn at the tap, otherwise $I_1\neq I_2$ (Stage 10).
A digital-to-analog converter (D/A converter) turns a number into a voltage.

Three bits (binary digits $b_0$, $b_1$, $b_2$) give the numbers $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Z}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$ to 7. A chain of $R/2$, seven $R$ and $R/2$ has the total resistance $8R$ and divides $U_\mathrm{ref}$ into eight steps.
A buffer, an amplifier with the factor 1, outputs the voltage without drawing current from the chain, so that the divider stays unloaded.
A comparator, a device that reports which of two voltages is higher, compares the input voltage with every tap, all at the same time.
A decoder, a logic circuit, turns the reports into the three-bit number.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 9.1 (Series connection and voltage divider)”?
karten.r:
$$\begin{aligned} I&=I_1=I_2=\dots=I_N,\qquad U=U_1+U_2+\dots+U_N,\qquad U_i=R_i\,I,\\ R_\mathrm{tot}&=\sum_{i=1}^{N}R_i,\qquad\frac{U_\nu}{U}=\frac{R_\nu}{\sum_{i=1}^NR_i}, \end{aligned}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{U_2}{U}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2},\qquad\frac{U_1}{U_2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_1}{R_2}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Total resistance and divider rule” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\begin{aligned} I&=I_1=I_2=\dots=I_N,\qquad U=U_1+U_2+\dots+U_N,\qquad U_i=R_i\,I,\\ R_\mathrm{tot}&=\sum_{i=1}^{N}R_i,\qquad\frac{U_\nu}{U}=\frac{R_\nu}{\sum_{i=1}^NR_i}, \end{aligned}$$
(9.1)(9.2)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{U_2}{U}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{U_1}{U_2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_1}{R_2}.}$$
(9.3)
karten.s0: The mesh rule gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sum U_i}$, Ohm's law gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_i\,I}$ with the same $I$.
s: So $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(R_1+\dots+R_N)\,I}$.
In the quotient of $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\nu}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\nu\,I}$ and $U$, $I$ cancels.

karten.r: The currents divide in the ratio of the conductances, the current divider.
The voltage of a divider is to supply another circuit stage; the load resistor $R_\mathrm L$ lies in parallel with $R_2$ (Fig. 11).

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 10.1 (Parallel connection and current divider)”?
karten.r:
$$\begin{aligned} U&=U_1=\dots=U_N,\qquad I=I_1+\dots+I_N,\qquad I_i=G_i\,U=\frac{U}{R_i},\\ G_\mathrm{tot}&=\frac{1}{R_\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}G_i=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{R_i},\qquad R_\mathrm{tot}=\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N\frac1{R_i}\Bigr)^{-1}. \end{aligned}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_1\parallel R_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_1\,R_2}{R_1+R_2},\qquad I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{tot}\,\frac{G_1}{G_1+G_2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{tot}\,\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2},\quad I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{tot}\,\frac{G_2}{G_1+G_2}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Total conductance and current divider” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\begin{aligned} U&=U_1=\dots=U_N,\qquad I=I_1+\dots+I_N,\qquad I_i=G_i\,U=\frac{U}{R_i},\\ G_\mathrm{tot}&=\frac{1}{R_\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}G_i=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{R_i},\qquad R_\mathrm{tot}=\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N\frac1{R_i}\Bigr)^{-1}. \end{aligned}$$
(10.1)(10.2)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_1\parallel R_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_1\,R_2}{R_1+R_2},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{tot}\,\frac{G_1}{G_1+G_2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{tot}\,\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2},\quad I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{tot}\,\frac{G_2}{G_1+G_2}.}$$
(10.3)
karten.s0: The node rule gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sum I_i}$, so with the same $U$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(G_1+\dots+G_N)\,U}$.

With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1/R}$,

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{tot}\,\frac{1/R_1}{1/R_1+1/R_2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{tot}\,\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}.}$$

karten.r: What remains is a small drift velocity (average velocity along the conductor) that is proportional to the field.

That is why the current density, the current per cross-sectional area, is proportional to the field, and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,I}$ follows for the component.
In series the voltage divides (voltage divider: two resistors whose ratio sets a partial voltage), in parallel the current divides.
Two metal plates with an insulator between them: this component is called a capacitor.
Each plate is an electrode; the insulator between them is called the dielectric.
The quantity that characterizes the component is the capacitance: it says how much charge sits on the plates per volt.
The basic form is two flat plates, the parallel-plate capacitor.
An RC circuit is the series connection of a resistor and a capacitor across a source.

karten.v: How can “Why the same current flows at both terminals” be derived?
karten.z: A capacitor consists of two electrodes separated by a dielectric. Its charge $Q$ is the charge of the positive electrode; the other carries $-Q$. Current through the capacitor means: a current flows in at one terminal, and at the same moment the same current flows out at the other.
karten.s0: Suppose more flows in than out.
s: Then a net charge $Q_\mathrm{n}$ collects in the component, and the whole component rises in potential relative to its surroundings.

How much is shown by a sphere the size of a housing, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{r}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1}$ cm: according to Chapter 1 it has the potential $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{k\,Q_\mathrm{n}/r}$, and just 1 µC would give 900 kV.
The field of this charge brakes the inflow long before a measurable difference arises.
So $Q_\mathrm{n}$ stays practically zero, and Kirchhoff's current law from Chapter 2 holds for the component as a whole.

karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{C}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{Q}{U},\qquad Q}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{C\,U,\qquad[C]}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{\mathrm{A\,s}}{\mathrm V}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm F\ \text{(farad)}.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 3.1 (Current and voltage at the capacitor)”?
karten.r: $$\begin{aligned} i(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d} q}{\mathrm{d} t}=C\,\frac{\mathrm{d} u(t)}{\mathrm{d} t},\\ u(t)&=\frac{q(t)}{C}=u(t_0)+\frac1C\int_{t_0}^{t}i(t')\,\mathrm{d} t'. \end{aligned}$$

karten.v: How can “Current and voltage” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\begin{aligned} i(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d} q}{\mathrm{d} t}=C\,\frac{\mathrm{d} u(t)}{\mathrm{d} t},\\ u(t)&=\frac{q(t)}{C}=u(t_0)+\frac1C\int_{t_0}^{t}i(t')\,\mathrm{d} t'. \end{aligned}$$
(3.1)(3.2)
karten.s0: Current is charge per time, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{d} q/\mathrm{d} t}$ (Chapter 2).
s: Substituting $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{q}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{C\,u}$ and pulling out the constant number $C$ gives (3.1).

Conversely, the charge is the area under the current curve, just as distance is the area under the velocity (Chapter 1): $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{q(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{q(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t}i\,\mathrm{d} t'}$.

karten.v: How can “From the field-line picture to the formula” be derived?
karten.z:
For two flat plates of area $A$ at separation $d$, with a dielectric filling the space,

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{C}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varepsilon\,\frac{A}{d},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varepsilon}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varepsilon_0\,\varepsilon_\mathrm{r},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varepsilon_0}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{8.854\cdot10^{-12}\,\frac{\mathrm{A\,s}}{\mathrm{V\,m}}.}$$
(4.1)
karten.s0:
A point charge produces the field $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{E}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0\cdot4\pi r^2}}$. The denominator contains the spherical surface through which all its field lines run. So, according to Chapter 1: The field strength is the charge, divided by $\varepsilon_0$ and by the area that its lines pass through uniformly. In the pair of plates, all lines of the charge $Q$ run in parallel through the area $A$:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{E}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0\,A},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{E\,d}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{Q\,d}{\varepsilon_0\,A}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac QU}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varepsilon_0\,\frac Ad.}$$
s: With a dielectric, lines end on the bound charge $Q_\mathrm{g}$, and only the share $Q-Q_\mathrm{g}$ still runs through the space. In most insulators this share is a fixed fraction of $Q$. One writes $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Q-Q_\mathrm{g}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q/\varepsilon_\mathrm{r}}$, which gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{E}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q/(\varepsilon_\mathrm{r}\varepsilon_0A)}$ and thus (4.1).

karten.v: How can “Energy from force and distance” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_0^Q\frac qC\,\mathrm{d} q}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{Q^2}{2C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,Q\,U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,C\,U^2.}$$
(6.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,\varepsilon\,E^2\cdot A\,d,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{w}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac WV}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,\varepsilon\,E^2.}$$
(6.2)
karten.s0: The force on $\Delta q$ in the field is $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{F}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\Delta q\,E}$ (Chapter 1). Over the distance $\Delta s$ between the plates, this costs $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\Delta W}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{F\,\Delta s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\Delta q\,E\,\Delta s}$. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{E\,\Delta s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{u}$ it follows that $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\Delta W}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\Delta q\,u}$, and with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{q/C}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\Delta W}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac qC\,\Delta q}$. For small $\Delta q$, the sum of all portions becomes the integral (6.1).
s: The circuit side gives the same result. The power (energy per time) is $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{p}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{u\,i}$ (Chapter 2). With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{C\,\mathrm{d} u/\mathrm{d} t}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int u\,i\,\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{C\int_0^Uu\,\mathrm{d} u}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12CU^2}$.

⁠From the component to the field: Substituting $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{C}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varepsilon A/d}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{E\,d}$ in (6.1) gives (6.2).

karten.s0: ⁠Parallel. Constraint of the circuit: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{G}}$ for all $i$. Individual charge: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Q_i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{C_iU_i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{C_iU_\mathrm{G}}$. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{C_\mathrm{G}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Q_\mathrm{G}/U_\mathrm{G}}$ the left formula follows.

karten.v: How can “Loss in the equalization” be derived?
karten.z: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W_\mathrm{V}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,\frac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2}\,(U_1-U_2)^2.}$$
karten.s0:
With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{C_1U_1+C_2U_2}{C_1+C_2}}$ from (8.1),

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W_\mathrm{V}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\tfrac12C_1U_1^2+\tfrac12C_2U_2^2-\tfrac12\,\frac{(C_1U_1+C_2U_2)^2}{C_1+C_2}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Solving the equation from the ground up” be derived?
karten.z:
For $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u_C(0)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$ and $t\ge0$,

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u_C(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_0\bigl(1-\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\bigr),}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{i(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_0}{R}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u_R(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,C.}$$
(9.3)
karten.s0:
⁠Step 1: Only the distance to the end counts. Let $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{x(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_0-u_C(t)}$. Because $U_0$ is constant, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathrm{d} x/\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\mathrm{d} u_C/\mathrm{d} t}$, and (9.2) becomes

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} t}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{x}{\tau},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{x(0)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_0.}$$
s: The change of $x$ is proportional to $x$ itself: the larger the remainder, the faster it shrinks.

⁠Step 2: Divide by $x$. For $x>0$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac1x\,\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} t}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac1\tau}$. By the chain rule the left side is the derivative of $\ln x(t)$, because $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}\ln x(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac1x\,\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} t}}$.
⁠Step 3: Integrate. So $\ln x(t)$ has the constant slope $-1/\tau$ and is a straight line: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\ln x(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-t/\tau+K}$ with a constant $K$.

⁠Step 4: Undo the logarithm. Applying the exponential function to both sides gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{x(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{e}^{K}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}}$. For $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$ this reads $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{x(0)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{e}^{K}}$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathrm{e}^{K}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_0}$. Thus $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{x(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}}$.

⁠Step 5: Convert back. $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u_C}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_0-x}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_0(1-\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau})}$. Differentiating: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{C\,\mathrm{d} u_C/\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{C\,U_0}{\tau}\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_0}{R}\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}}$, and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u_R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,i}$.

⁠Verification: Substituting into (9.1) gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R\,C\cdot\frac{U_0}{\tau}\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}+U_0-U_0\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_0}$. It checks out.

⁠The same route via the current: From $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_0}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,i+\frac1C\int_0^ti\,\mathrm{d} t'}$, differentiating gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{0}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,\frac{\mathrm{d} i}{\mathrm{d} t}+\frac iC}$. Written briefly this is $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{\mathrm{d} i}{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{\mathrm{d} t}{RC}}$, and steps 2 to 4 give $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\ln i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{t}{RC}+\ln\frac{U_0}{R}}$, so again $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_0}{R}\mathrm{e}^{-t/RC}}$.

karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u_C(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau},\qquad i(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{U_0}{R}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau},\qquad u_R(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-U_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 3.1 (Error of the ammeter)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac UR,\qquad I_R'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U}{R+R_\mathrm i}<I_R,\qquad \frac{I_R}{I_R'}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R+R_\mathrm i}{R}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1+\frac{R_\mathrm i}{R}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Error of the ammeter” be derived?
karten.z:
Without a meter, $I_R$ flows; with a meter, $I_R'$:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac UR,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_R'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U}{R+R_\mathrm i}<I_R,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{I_R}{I_R'}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R+R_\mathrm i}{R}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1+\frac{R_\mathrm i}{R}.}$$
(3.1)

The relative error is $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{f}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(I_R'-I_R)/I_R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-R_\mathrm i/(R+R_\mathrm i)}$. For $R_\mathrm i\ll R$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{f}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-R_\mathrm i/R}$.
karten.s0: The mesh rule reads $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_R'R+I_R'R_\mathrm i}$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_R'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U/(R+R_\mathrm i)}$.
s: Hence $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{f}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_R'/I_R-1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R/(R+R_\mathrm i)-1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-R_\mathrm i/(R+R_\mathrm i)}$.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 4.1 (Error of the voltmeter)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_L'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm q\,(R_L\parallel R_\mathrm i)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_L\cdot\frac{1}{1+R_L/R_\mathrm i}.}$$

karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_L'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm q\,(R_L\parallel R_\mathrm i)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_L\cdot\frac{1}{1+R_L/R_\mathrm i}.}$$
(4.1)
karten.s0: With the node rule $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm q}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_{RL}'+I_{\mathrm{i}}}$, the current divides between two parallel resistors, and $U_L'$ is across both.
s: So $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_L'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm q\,R_LR_\mathrm i/(R_L+R_\mathrm i)}$, and canceling $R_\mathrm i$ gives (4.1).
On the divider, without a meter $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U\,R_2/(R_1+R_2)}$.

With a meter, $R_2$ is replaced by $R_2\parallel R_\mathrm i$ (loaded voltage divider, Chapter 2):

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_2'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U\,\frac{R_2R_\mathrm i}{R_1R_2+R_\mathrm i(R_1+R_2)} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{U_2'}{U_2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_\mathrm i(R_1+R_2)}{R_1R_2+R_\mathrm i(R_1+R_2)}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{1+(R_1\parallel R_2)/R_\mathrm i}.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 5.1 (Correct-current and correct-voltage measurement)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac UI}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R+R_\mathrm{iA},\qquad f}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{+\frac{R_\mathrm{iA}}{R}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac UI}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\parallel R_\mathrm{iV},\qquad f}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{R}{R+R_\mathrm{iV}}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Quotient of the readings” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac UI}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R+R_\mathrm{iA},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{f}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{+\frac{R_\mathrm{iA}}{R}.}$$
(5.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac UI}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\parallel R_\mathrm{iV},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{f}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{R}{R+R_\mathrm{iV}}.}$$
(5.2)
karten.s0: Correct current: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U/I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(I_RR+I_RR_\mathrm{iA})/I_R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R+R_\mathrm{iA}}$.
s: Correct voltage: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I/U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(I_R+I_\mathrm{iV})/U_R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1/R+1/R_\mathrm{iV}}$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U/I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\parallel R_\mathrm{iV}}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{f}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(R\parallel R_\mathrm{iV})/R-1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-R/(R+R_\mathrm{iV})}$.

karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_4}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_3\,\frac{R_2}{R_1}.}$$

karten.z:
If no current flows through the instrument,

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_4}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_3\,\frac{R_2}{R_1}.}$$
(6.1)
karten.s0: Without a cross current, the node rule gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_2}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_3}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_4}$.
s: Equal potentials of the midpoints give $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_{R2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_{R4}}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_{R1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_{R3}}$.

So

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{U_{R4}}{U_{R3}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_{R2}}{U_{R1}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{I_4R_4}{I_3R_3}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_2R_2}{I_1R_1} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{R_4}{R_3}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_2}{R_1}.}$$

karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm d}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm q\left(\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}-\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}\right)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm q\,\frac{R_1R_4-R_2R_3}{(R_1+R_2)(R_3+R_4)}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm d}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm q}{4}\cdot\frac{\Delta R/R}{1+\Delta R/(2R)}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm q}{4}\cdot\frac{\Delta R}{R}\qquad\text{for }\Delta R\ll R.}$$

karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm d}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm q\left(\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}-\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}\right)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm q\,\frac{R_1R_4-R_2R_3}{(R_1+R_2)(R_3+R_4)}.}$$
(7.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm d}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm q}{4}\cdot\frac{\Delta R/R}{1+\Delta R/(2R)}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm q}{4}\cdot\frac{\Delta R}{R}}$$
$$\text{for }\Delta R\ll R.$$
(7.2)
s:
With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm q/2}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_4}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm q(R+\Delta R)/(2R+\Delta R)}$,

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm d}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm q\,\frac{2(R+\Delta R)-(2R+\Delta R)}{2(2R+\Delta R)}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm q\,\Delta R}{4R+2\Delta R}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm q}{4}\cdot\frac{\Delta R/R}{1+\Delta R/(2R)}.}$$

karten.r: An ammeter (current meter) sits in series in the circuit and adds its internal resistance to it.
A voltmeter (voltage meter) sits in parallel and opens a second current path.

karten.v: What does “correct-current measurement, correct-voltage measurement” mean?
karten.r: If both measure at once, only one reading is right: correct-current measurement (the current is right) or correct-voltage measurement (the voltage is right).
The Wheatstone bridge (two voltage dividers on one source with an instrument between them) compares resistances.
At balance (adjusted to a reading of zero), no current flows through the instrument.
A terminal is a connection point to the outside.
A series-parallel circuit consists of series and parallel groups nested inside one another.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{a}+R_\mathrm{b}\parallel\bigl(R_\mathrm{c}+R_\mathrm{d}\parallel R_\mathrm{e}\parallel R_\mathrm{f}\bigr) }\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{a}+\left[G_\mathrm{b}+\frac{1}{R_\mathrm{c}+\dfrac{1}{G_\mathrm{d}+G_\mathrm{e}+G_\mathrm{f}}}\right]^{-1}.}$$
You may connect all of them and calculate only one side, the half circuit.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 2.1 (Two symmetry rules)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{2\,R_\mathrm{A,axis}.}$$

karten.v: How can “The potentials follow from the symmetry” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{2\,R_\mathrm{A,axis}.}$$
(2.1)
karten.s0: Rule 1: The mirrored network has the same components, the same terminals and the same voltage, hence the same equations. These have exactly one solution. Two nodes that coincide must therefore have the same potential.
s: Rule 2: Let the reference point lie in the middle, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{+\frac12U}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac12U}$. Mirroring swaps A and B, so it acts like reversing the polarity of the voltage. In a linear network, reversing the polarity inverts every potential (Stage 8). For a point $P$ and its mirror image $P'$, therefore, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi(P')}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\varphi(P)}$. A point on the axis is its own mirror image, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\varphi}$ and thus $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, the mean value. The two halves are equal and in series, which gives (2.1).

karten.r: A delta is three resistors between three terminals.
A star is three resistors from three terminals to a common inner node, the star point.

karten.v: What does “$\pi$ network, T network” mean?
karten.r: The delta is then called a $\pi$ network, the star a T network.

karten.v: How can “Star to delta, then invert” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_{10}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_{12}R_{31}}{R_{12}+R_{23}+R_{31}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_{20}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_{12}R_{23}}{R_{12}+R_{23}+R_{31}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_{30}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_{23}R_{31}}{R_{12}+R_{23}+R_{31}}.}$$
(3.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{G_{10}G_{20}}{G_{10}+G_{20}+G_{30}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G_{23}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{G_{20}G_{30}}{G_{10}+G_{20}+G_{30}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G_{31}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{G_{30}G_{10}}{G_{10}+G_{20}+G_{30}}.}$$
(3.2)
karten.s0:
In the star, the node rule at the star point reads $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G_{10}(\varphi_1-\varphi_0)+G_{20}(\varphi_2-\varphi_0)+G_{30}(\varphi_3-\varphi_0)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{S}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{G_{10}+G_{20}+G_{30}}$ it follows that $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi_0}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(G_{10}\varphi_1+G_{20}\varphi_2+G_{30}\varphi_3)/S}$. The current into terminal 1 is thus

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{G_{10}(\varphi_1-\varphi_0)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{G_{10}G_{20}}{S}(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)+\frac{G_{10}G_{30}}{S}(\varphi_1-\varphi_3).}$$
s: In the delta, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{G_{12}(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)+G_{31}(\varphi_1-\varphi_3)}$. Comparing the two gives (3.2), for arbitrary potentials. Terminal 2 gives $G_{23}$ in the same way.

For the inversion, let $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{H}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_{10}R_{20}+R_{20}R_{30}+R_{30}R_{10}}$. Then $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{S}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{H/(R_{10}R_{20}R_{30})}$, and (3.2) becomes $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{H/R_{30}}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_{23}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{H/R_{10}}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_{31}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{H/R_{20}}$. From these follow $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_{12}R_{31}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{H^2/(R_{20}R_{30})}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_{12}+R_{23}+R_{31}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{H^2/(R_{10}R_{20}R_{30})}$. The quotient is $R_{10}$, which is (3.1).

karten.r: An ideal voltage source holds the potential difference between its terminals.
An ideal current source holds the current in its branch.

karten.v: What does “source voltage, source current” mean?
karten.r: $U_\mathrm{q}$ is the source voltage in V, from millivolts to kilovolts, here 9 V. $I_\mathrm{q}$ is the source current in A, from microamperes to amperes.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}\quad\text{for every current},\qquad\qquad I_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{q}\quad\text{for every voltage}.}$$
An equivalent circuit is a circuit of ideal elements that behaves like the real component at the terminals.

karten.v: What does “real voltage source, real current source” mean?
karten.r: The real voltage source is an ideal voltage source in series with $R_\mathrm{q}$, the real current source an ideal current source in parallel with $G_\mathrm{q}$.

A load imposes a second equation, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{L}I_\mathrm{A}}$. This straight line through the origin is called the load line.
Both equations must hold at once. That is possible only at the intersection, the operating point.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}-R_\mathrm{q}\,I_\mathrm{A}, \qquad\qquad I_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{q}-G_\mathrm{q}\,U_\mathrm{AB}.}$$
Two networks are called equivalent if they have the same characteristic curves.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 6.1 (Equivalence of real sources)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{q}}{G_\mathrm{q}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad R_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{G_\mathrm{q}}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Equating the lines” be derived?
karten.z:
A real voltage source and a real current source are equivalent if

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{q}}{G_\mathrm{q}}}$$
$$\text{and}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{G_\mathrm{q}}.}$$
(6.1)
karten.s0:
You solve the current-source equation from (5.1) for the voltage, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(I_\mathrm{q}-I_\mathrm{A})/G_\mathrm{q}}$, and equate it with the voltage-source equation:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{I_\mathrm{q}}{G_\mathrm{q}}-\frac{I_\mathrm{A}}{G_\mathrm{q}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}-R_\mathrm{q}I_\mathrm{A}.}$$
s: This must hold for every current. So the terms without $I_\mathrm{A}$ and the terms with $I_\mathrm{A}$ must be equal separately. That is (6.1).

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 7.1 (Interconnecting real sources)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{eq}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q1}+U_\mathrm{q2},\quad R_\mathrm{eq}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{q1}+R_\mathrm{q2} \qquad\text{or}\qquad I_\mathrm{eq}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{q1}+I_\mathrm{q2},\quad G_\mathrm{eq}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{G_\mathrm{q1}+G_\mathrm{q2}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{eq}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{G_\mathrm{q1}U_\mathrm{q1}+G_\mathrm{q2}U_\mathrm{q2}}{G_\mathrm{q1}+G_\mathrm{q2}},\qquad R_\mathrm{eq}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{q1}\parallel R_\mathrm{q2}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Parallel in the current-source form” be derived?
karten.z: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{circ}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q1}-U_\mathrm{q2}}{R_\mathrm{q1}+R_\mathrm{q2}}.}$$
karten.s0: Both sources have the voltage $U_\mathrm{AB}$, and the node rule adds their currents: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(I_\mathrm{q1}-G_\mathrm{q1}U_\mathrm{AB})+(I_\mathrm{q2}-G_\mathrm{q2}U_\mathrm{AB})}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(I_\mathrm{q1}+I_\mathrm{q2})-(G_\mathrm{q1}+G_\mathrm{q2})U_\mathrm{AB}}$.
s: This is again the form from (5.1).
With (6.1), (7.2) follows.
In series, the mesh rule adds the voltages in the same way.
The circulating current is the loop voltage $U_\mathrm{q1}-U_\mathrm{q2}$ divided by the resistance of the loop.

karten.r: A source is independent if its value depends on no quantity in the network.
$a_k$ is the voltage gain from source $k$ to the voltage $U_\mathrm{AB}$, without a unit: this is how many volts $U_\mathrm{AB}$ changes per volt of the source. It is also called the sensitivity.

$$\begin{aligned} U_\mathrm{AB}&=a_1U_\mathrm{q1}+\dots+a_nU_{\mathrm{q}n}+Z_1I_\mathrm{q1}+\dots+Z_mI_{\mathrm{q}m},\\ I_\mathrm{CD}&=Y_1U_\mathrm{q1}+\dots+Y_nU_{\mathrm{q}n}+b_1I_\mathrm{q1}+\dots+b_mI_{\mathrm{q}m}. \end{aligned}$$

karten.v: How can “The coefficients of N” be derived?
karten.s0:
With the terminals open, the node rule at A reads $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{(U_\mathrm{q1}-U_\mathrm{AB})/R_1+I_\mathrm{q2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{AB}/R_2}$. Solved for the voltage we want:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}\,U_\mathrm{q1}+\frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}\,I_\mathrm{q2}.}$$
s: This is the form (8.1): each term belongs to one source, and the coefficients contain only resistors.

karten.v: What does “equivalent voltage source, equivalent current source” mean?
karten.r: Every linear one-port behaves at its terminals like an equivalent voltage source and equally like an equivalent current source.
The straight line is also called the load characteristic.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 9.1 (Equivalent sources: Thevenin and Norton)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{i}-R_\mathrm{i}\,I_\mathrm{A},\qquad\qquad I_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{i}-G_\mathrm{i}\,U_\mathrm{AB},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{OC},\qquad I_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{SC},\qquad R_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{G_\mathrm{i}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{OC}}{I_\mathrm{SC}}.}$$

karten.v: How can “The straight line from superposition” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{i}-R_\mathrm{i}\,I_\mathrm{A},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{i}-G_\mathrm{i}\,U_\mathrm{AB},}$$
(9.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{OC},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{SC},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{G_\mathrm{i}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{OC}}{I_\mathrm{SC}}.}$$
(9.2)
karten.s0:
With the imagined current source $I_\mathrm{A}$ at the terminals, (8.1) gives

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\underbrace{\sum_k a_kU_{\mathrm{q}k}+\sum_k Z_kI_{\mathrm{q}k}}_{\text{internal sources}}\;\underbrace{-\,R_\mathrm{i}I_\mathrm{A}}_{\text{terminal current}}.}$$
s: For $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$ the first part remains, so it is $U_\mathrm{OC}$. With all internal sources turned off, the second part remains: there $R_\mathrm{i}$ is the total resistance of the turned-off network between A and B. The minus comes from the reference arrow: $I_\mathrm{A}$ flows out of A, so inside from B to A, with A lower. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{AB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{SC}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{OC}/R_\mathrm{i}}$. Rearranging gives the second form.
