karten.v: How can “Equivalent source from left to right” be derived?
karten.z:
For the converter in Fig. 12 with the output open,

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{out}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{ref}\left(\frac{d_2}{2}+\frac{d_1}{4}+\frac{d_0}{8}\right),}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R.}$$
(10.1)
karten.s0:
At the left node, 2$R$ lies against ground and 2$R$ against $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_0}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{d_0U_\mathrm{ref}}$. This is an equivalent source with $\frac12U_0$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{2R\parallel2R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R}$. With the series resistor it becomes $\frac12U_0$ and $2R$. At the next node this meets 2$R$ against $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{d_1U_\mathrm{ref}}$: again two equal branches, hence the averaging from (7.2), the equivalent source $\frac12\bigl(\frac12U_0+U_1\bigr)$ and again $R$. The last node repeats this:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{out}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\tfrac12\Bigl(\tfrac12\bigl(\tfrac12U_0+U_1\bigr)+U_2\Bigr)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\tfrac12U_2+\tfrac14U_1+\tfrac18U_0.}$$
s: Superposition gives the same number. Take source $U_1$ as an example: at the middle node it sees 2$R$ on the left and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R+2R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{3R}$ on the right, together $\frac65R$. The divider gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{6/5}{6/5+2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac38U_1}$ there. The way to the output divides once more by $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{2R}{R+2R}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac23}$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac38\cdot\frac23}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac14}$.

karten.r: The sources set the open-circuit voltage $U_\mathrm{OC}$ (the voltage with the terminals open), the resistors set the internal resistance $R_\mathrm{i}$ (the slope).
A straight line has two numbers. So the network behaves like an equivalent source, a source with an internal resistance.
A network with two such terminal pairs is called a two-port, and each terminal pair is a port.
A controlled source supplies a value proportional to another voltage or another current elsewhere in the circuit.
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, here almost always with two rows and two columns.
The number $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\det\mathbf M}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{a\,d-b\,c}$ is called the determinant.
The product $\mathbf M\,\mathbf M^{-1}$ is the identity matrix $\mathbf 1$ with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
A four-pole is a network with four terminals.
The historical name four-pole lives on in four-pole theory.
Usually a source is connected to port 1, the input, and a load to port 2, the output.

karten.v: What does “forward direction, reverse direction” mean?
karten.r: Energy then flows in the forward direction $1\to2$; the opposite direction is called the reverse direction.
If a two-port has a continuous line from terminal 1$'$ to 2$'$, the ground line, it is called unbalanced (Fig. 2 left).
A two-port that, like the bridge circuit, has no such line and is built as a mirror image about a center line is called balanced.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 1.1 (Four-pole, port, two-port)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1+I_{1'}+I_2+I_{2'}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0,\qquad U_{11'}+U_{1'2'}-U_{22'}+U_{21}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_{1'}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-I_1,\qquad I_{2'}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-I_2.}$$
In the chain-arrow system, also called the technical arrow system, it applies only at the input; at the output the active sign convention applies: The output current points out, toward the load.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{f_1(U_1,U_2),\quad I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{g_1(U_1,U_2)\qquad\text{or}\qquad U_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{f_2(I_1,I_2),\quad U_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{g_2(I_1,I_2).}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{y_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{p_{11}x_1+p_{12}x_2,\qquad y_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{p_{21}x_1+p_{22}x_2.}$$
The Z parameters follow from two open-circuit tests.
Parameters with equal indices are called two-terminal quantities: They are the resistance of a terminal pair with the other side fixed in its termination.
Parameters with different indices are called transfer quantities: They link the two sides.
The letter $Z$ stands for impedance.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 3.1 (Impedance form, Z form)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{11}I_1+Z_{12}I_2,\quad U_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{21}I_1+Z_{22}I_2,\qquad\text{in short}\quad\mathbf U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf Z\cdot\mathbf I,\quad\mathbf Z}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\begin{pmatrix}Z_{11}&Z_{12}\\mathbb{Z}_{21}&Z_{22}\end{pmatrix}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Z_{11}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{U_1}{I_1}\right|_{I_2=0},\quad Z_{21}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{U_2}{I_1}\right|_{I_2=0},\quad Z_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{U_1}{I_2}\right|_{I_1=0},\quad Z_{22}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{U_2}{I_2}\right|_{I_1=0}.}$$
Less drops across $R_\mathrm{b}$, $U_1$ falls, and the input looks lower in resistance. This effect of the output on the input is called reverse action.
If $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Z_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, it is zero: The input notices nothing of the load, and the two-port is called unilateral.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 4.1 (Input resistance and output side)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{Z_{21}}{Z_{22}+Z_\mathrm{L}}\,I_1,\qquad Z_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_1}{I_1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{11}-\frac{Z_{12}Z_{21}}{Z_{22}+Z_\mathrm{L}}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Z_{1,\mathrm{OC}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{11},\qquad Z_{1,\mathrm{SC}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{11}-\frac{Z_{12}Z_{21}}{Z_{22}}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{Z_{21}}{Z_{11}+R_\mathrm{q}}\,U_\mathrm{q},\qquad R_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{22}-\frac{Z_{12}Z_{21}}{Z_{11}+R_\mathrm{q}}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Input resistance and output side” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{Z_{21}}{Z_{22}+Z_\mathrm{L}}\,I_1,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Z_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_1}{I_1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{11}-\frac{Z_{12}Z_{21}}{Z_{22}+Z_\mathrm{L}}.}$$
(4.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Z_{1,\mathrm{OC}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{11},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Z_{1,\mathrm{SC}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{11}-\frac{Z_{12}Z_{21}}{Z_{22}}.}$$
(4.2)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{Z_{21}}{Z_{11}+R_\mathrm{q}}\,U_\mathrm{q},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{22}-\frac{Z_{12}Z_{21}}{Z_{11}+R_\mathrm{q}}.}$$
(4.3)
karten.s0: Right mesh: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{21}I_1+Z_{22}I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-Z_\mathrm{L}I_2}$; solving for $I_2$ gives the first part of (4.1). Substituting into the left mesh $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{11}I_1+Z_{12}I_2}$ and dividing by $I_1$ gives $Z_1$. For $Z_\mathrm{L}\to\infty$ the fraction vanishes; for $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Z_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, $Z_{1,\mathrm{SC}}$ follows with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-Z_{21}I_1/Z_{22}}$.
s: For (4.3) you replace the load. The source imposes $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}-R_\mathrm{q}I_1}$. At $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}/(Z_{11}+R_\mathrm{q})}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{i}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{21}I_1}$. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, port 1 is terminated by $R_\mathrm{q}$, and $R_\mathrm{i}$ is $Z_1$ with swapped indices.

karten.r: The Y parameters follow from two short-circuit tests.

$Y$ stands for admittance, the reciprocal of impedance; here these are real conductances in siemens, typically micro- to millisiemens, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Y_{ii}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{G_{ii}}$.

karten.v: What does “short-circuit input conductance, short-circuit output conductance” mean?
karten.r: $Y_{11}$ is the short-circuit input conductance, $Y_{22}$ the short-circuit output conductance.

karten.v: What does “input characteristic, transfer characteristic, output characteristic” mean?
karten.r: The input characteristic is $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{f_1(U_1)}$ at fixed $U_2$, the transfer characteristic $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{f_2(U_1)}$ at fixed $U_2$, the output characteristic $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{f_3(U_2)}$ at fixed $U_1$.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 5.1 (Admittance form, Y form)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Y_{11}U_1+Y_{12}U_2,\quad I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Y_{21}U_1+Y_{22}U_2,\qquad\text{in short}\quad\mathbf I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf Y\cdot\mathbf U,\quad\mathbf Y}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\begin{pmatrix}Y_{11}&Y_{12}\\Y_{21}&Y_{22}\end{pmatrix}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Y_{11}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{I_1}{U_1}\right|_{U_2=0},\quad Y_{21}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{I_2}{U_1}\right|_{U_2=0},\quad Y_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{I_1}{U_2}\right|_{U_1=0},\quad Y_{22}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{I_2}{U_2}\right|_{U_1=0}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{Y_{21}}{Y_{22}+Y_\mathrm{L}}\,U_1,\qquad Y_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_1}{U_1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Y_{11}-\frac{Y_{12}Y_{21}}{Y_{22}+Y_\mathrm{L}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Y_{1,\mathrm{SC}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Y_{11},\qquad Y_{1,\mathrm{OC}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Y_{11}-\frac{Y_{12}Y_{21}}{Y_{22}}.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 6.1 (Conversion between Z and Y)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathbf Y}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf Z^{-1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{\det\mathbf Z}\begin{pmatrix}Z_{22}&-Z_{12}\\-Z_{21}&Z_{11}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf Z}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf Y^{-1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{\det\mathbf Y}\begin{pmatrix}Y_{22}&-Y_{12}\\-Y_{21}&Y_{11}\end{pmatrix}}$$

karten.v: How can “Two ways to the inverse” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathbf Y}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf Z^{-1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{\det\mathbf Z}\begin{pmatrix}Z_{22}&-Z_{12}\\-Z_{21}&Z_{11}\end{pmatrix},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathbf Z}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf Y^{-1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{\det\mathbf Y}\begin{pmatrix}Y_{22}&-Y_{12}\\-Y_{21}&Y_{11}\end{pmatrix}}$$
(6.1)
karten.s0: ⁠With matrices. From $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathbf I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf Y\mathbf U}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathbf U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf Z\mathbf I}$ follows $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathbf I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf Y\mathbf Z\,\mathbf I}$ for every $\mathbf I$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathbf Y\mathbf Z}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf 1}$.
s:
⁠With short-circuit tests on the Z equivalent circuit. At $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Z_{21}I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-Z_{22}I_2}$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{Z_{21}}{Z_{22}}I_1}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\bigl(Z_{11}-Z_{12}\frac{Z_{21}}{Z_{22}}\bigr)I_1}$. This gives

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Y_{11}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_1}{U_1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{Z_{22}}{Z_{11}Z_{22}-Z_{12}Z_{21}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Y_{21}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_2}{U_1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{Z_{21}}{Z_{11}Z_{22}-Z_{12}Z_{21}}.}$$

At $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{-Z_{11}I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{Z_{12}I_2}$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{Z_{12}}{Z_{11}}I_2}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\bigl(Z_{22}-Z_{21}\frac{Z_{12}}{Z_{11}}\bigr)I_2}$. This gives

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Y_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{Z_{12}}{Z_{11}Z_{22}-Z_{12}Z_{21}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{Y_{22}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{Z_{11}}{Z_{11}Z_{22}-Z_{12}Z_{21}}.}$$

karten.r: $H_{11}$ is the short-circuit input resistance in $\Omega$, typically a few k$\Omega$ for the transistor.

karten.v: What does “short-circuit current ratio, open-circuit reverse voltage ratio” mean?
karten.r: $H_{21}$ is the forward short-circuit current ratio, the current gain, without a unit, about 100 to 500. $H_{12}$ is the open-circuit reverse voltage ratio, without a unit, around $10^{-4}$.
$H_{22}$ is the open-circuit output conductance in S, a few tens of µ S. The units are mixed, hence the name.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 7.1 (Hybrid form, H form)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{H_{11}I_1+H_{12}U_2,\quad I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{H_{21}I_1+H_{22}U_2,\qquad\text{in short}\quad \begin{pmatrix}U_1\\I_2\end{pmatrix}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf H\begin{pmatrix}I_1\\U_2\end{pmatrix}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{H_{11}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{U_1}{I_1}\right|_{U_2=0},\quad H_{21}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{I_2}{I_1}\right|_{U_2=0},\quad H_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{U_1}{U_2}\right|_{I_1=0},\quad H_{22}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{I_2}{U_2}\right|_{I_1=0}.}$$
The A parameters follow from tests at the output.
For two two-ports in a chain, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathbf A}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf A'\mathbf A''}$.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 8.1 (Chain form, A form)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A_{11}U_2+A_{12}(-I_2),\quad I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A_{21}U_2+A_{22}(-I_2),\qquad\text{in short}\quad \begin{pmatrix}U_1\\I_1\end{pmatrix}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf A\begin{pmatrix}U_2\\-I_2\end{pmatrix}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{A_{11}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{U_1}{U_2}\right|_{I_2=0},\quad A_{21}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{I_1}{U_2}\right|_{I_2=0},\quad A_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.-\frac{U_1}{I_2}\right|_{U_2=0},\quad A_{22}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.-\frac{I_1}{I_2}\right|_{U_2=0}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Why the chain is a matrix product” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A_{11}U_2+A_{12}(-I_2),\quad I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A_{21}U_2+A_{22}(-I_2),}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\text{in short}\quad \begin{pmatrix}U_1\\I_1\end{pmatrix}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathbf A\begin{pmatrix}U_2\\-I_2\end{pmatrix}.}$$
(8.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{A_{11}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{U_1}{U_2}\right|_{I_2=0},\quad A_{21}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.\frac{I_1}{U_2}\right|_{I_2=0},\quad A_{12}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.-\frac{U_1}{I_2}\right|_{U_2=0},\quad A_{22}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left.-\frac{I_1}{I_2}\right|_{U_2=0}.}$$
(8.2)
karten.s0: One prime marks the first two-port, two primes the second.

karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{p(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{\mathrm{d} W}{\mathrm{d} t}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{u(t)\,i(t),\qquad W}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int u\,\mathrm{d} Q}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\int_{t_1}^{t_2}u(t)\,i(t)\,\mathrm{d} t.}$$

karten.v: How can “Why only voltage and current count” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{p(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{\mathrm{d} W}{\mathrm{d} t}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{u(t)\,i(t),}$$

(1.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{W}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U\,I\,\Delta t,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{W}{\Delta t}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U\,I.}$$

karten.v: How can “From collisions to $U^2/R$” be derived?
karten.z:
In a resistor, all the electrical power turns into heat:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U\,I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,I^2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U^2}{R}.}$$
(2.1)

A component tolerates this only up to its power rating $P_\mathrm{max}$:

$$P\le P_\mathrm{max}.$$
(2.2)
karten.s0:
In the model from Chapter 2, an electron is accelerated at $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{a}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{e\,E/m_\mathrm e}$ and reaches $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{v_\mathrm{max}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{a\,T}$ over the distance $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12a\,T^2}$. The field does the work $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{e\,E\,s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{m_\mathrm e\,a\,s}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12m_\mathrm e(a\,T)^2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{W_1}$, exactly the kinetic energy at the collision. The volume $A\,L$ contains $n\,A\,L$ free electrons, and each collides $1/T$ times per second:

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{n\,A\,L\,\frac{W_1}{T}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{n\,A\,L\,\frac{e^2E^2\,T}{2\,m_\mathrm e}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\sigma\,E^2\,A\,L.}$$
s: Here $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\sigma}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{n\,e\,\mu}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mu}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{e\,T/(2\,m_\mathrm e)}$ (Chapter 2). With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{E\,L}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{L/(\sigma A)}$, this becomes $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U^2/R}$.

karten.r: $\hat u$ and $\hat\imath$ are the amplitudes, the peak values.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 3.1 (Average power at a resistor)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac1T\int_0^T u(t)\,i(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,\frac{\hat u^2}{R}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,\hat\imath^2R.}$$

karten.v: How can “Where the factor $\frac12$ comes from” be derived?
karten.z:
For $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\hat u\cos(\omega t)}$ across $R$, the current $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{i(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\hat\imath\cos(\omega t)}$ flows with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\hat\imath}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\hat u/R}$. The time average of the power is

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac1T\int_0^T u(t)\,i(t)\,\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,\frac{\hat u^2}{R}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,\hat\imath^2R.}$$
(3.1)
karten.s0:
Substituting gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{p}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{u\,i}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{u^2/R}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(\hat u^2/R)\cos^2(\omega t)}$. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\cos^2x}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12(1+\cos2x)}$, this becomes

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{T\,R}\int_0^T\hat u^2\cos^2(\omega t)\,\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{T\,R}\int_0^T\hat u^2\,\frac12\bigl(1+\cos(2\omega t)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,\frac{\hat u^2}{R}.}$$
s: The cosine part goes through two full oscillations in $T$; its integral is zero. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\hat u}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,\hat\imath}$, the second form follows.

karten.r: $U_\mathrm{cable}$ is the voltage drop along the line.

karten.v: What does “power loss, useful power” mean?
karten.r: $P_\mathrm{cable}$ is the power loss, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{useful}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{P_\mathrm{L}}$ the useful power of the load, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}I}$ the power of the source.
The nominal voltage is the voltage for which a grid is designed.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{cable}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{cable}\,I,\qquad P_\mathrm{cable}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{cable}\,I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{cable}\,I^2,\qquad P_\mathrm{useful}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(U_\mathrm{q}-U_\mathrm{cable})\,I}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{P_\mathrm{useful}}{P_\mathrm{q}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{(U_\mathrm{q}-U_\mathrm{cable})\,I}{U_\mathrm{q}\,I}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1-\frac{U_\mathrm{cable}}{U_\mathrm{q}}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{I_1}{I_2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{L2}}{U_\mathrm{L1}},\qquad\frac{P_\mathrm{cable,1}}{P_\mathrm{cable,2}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left(\frac{U_\mathrm{L2}}{U_\mathrm{L1}}\right)^{\!2}.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 5.1 (Power balance and efficiency)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}\,I,\qquad P_\mathrm{v}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{Ri}\,I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I^2R_\mathrm{i},\qquad P_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{L}\,I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I^2R_\mathrm{L},\qquad P_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{P_\mathrm{v}+P_\mathrm{L}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\eta}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{P_\mathrm{L}}{P_\mathrm{q}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I\,U_\mathrm{L}}{I\,U_\mathrm{q}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{L}}{U_\mathrm{q}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_\mathrm{L}}{R_\mathrm{L}+R_\mathrm{i}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_\mathrm{L}/R_\mathrm{i}}{1+R_\mathrm{L}/R_\mathrm{i}}.}$$

karten.v: How can “The balance is the mesh rule times the current” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}\,I,}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{v}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{Ri}\,I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I^2R_\mathrm{i},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{L}\,I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I^2R_\mathrm{L},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{P_\mathrm{v}+P_\mathrm{L}.}$$
(5.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\eta}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{P_\mathrm{L}}{P_\mathrm{q}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I\,U_\mathrm{L}}{I\,U_\mathrm{q}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{L}}{U_\mathrm{q}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_\mathrm{L}}{R_\mathrm{L}+R_\mathrm{i}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{R_\mathrm{L}/R_\mathrm{i}}{1+R_\mathrm{L}/R_\mathrm{i}}.}$$
(5.2)
karten.s0: The mesh rule reads $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{Ri}+U_\mathrm{L}}$.
s: Multiplied by $I$, it gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{P_\mathrm{v}+P_\mathrm{L}}$.
In (5.2), $I$ cancels, because both resistors carry the same current.
The voltage divider (Chapter 2) gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}\,R_\mathrm{L}/(R_\mathrm{L}+R_\mathrm{i})}$.

karten.r: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{SC}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}I_\mathrm{SC}}$ is the short-circuit power, the power of the source at $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{L}(R_\mathrm{L})}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left(\frac{U_\mathrm{q}}{R_\mathrm{i}+R_\mathrm{L}}\right)^{\!2}R_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}^2\,\frac{R_\mathrm{L}}{\bigl(R_\mathrm{i}(1+R_\mathrm{L}/R_\mathrm{i})\bigr)^2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{P_\mathrm{SC}\,\frac{\alpha}{(1+\alpha)^2},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{i},\qquad P_\mathrm{L,max}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q}^2}{4\,R_\mathrm{i}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{P_\mathrm{SC}}{4},\qquad I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{SC}}{2},\qquad U_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q}}{2}.}$$

karten.v: How can “The maximum, in three ways” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{L}(R_\mathrm{L})}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\left(\frac{U_\mathrm{q}}{R_\mathrm{i}+R_\mathrm{L}}\right)^{\!2}R_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{q}^2\,\frac{R_\mathrm{L}}{\bigl(R_\mathrm{i}(1+R_\mathrm{L}/R_\mathrm{i})\bigr)^2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{P_\mathrm{SC}\,\frac{\alpha}{(1+\alpha)^2},}$$
(6.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{i},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{L,max}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q}^2}{4\,R_\mathrm{i}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{P_\mathrm{SC}}{4},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{SC}}{2},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q}}{2}.}$$
(6.2)
karten.s0:
By the quotient rule, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\bigl(f/g\bigr)'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(f'g-f\,g')/g^2}$, with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{f}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\alpha}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{g}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(1+\alpha)^2}$,

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{\mathrm{d} P_\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{P_\mathrm{SC}\,\frac{(1+\alpha)^2-2\alpha(1+\alpha)}{(1+\alpha)^4}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{P_\mathrm{SC}\,\frac{1-\alpha}{(1+\alpha)^3}.}$$
s: The derivative is zero at $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\alpha}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1}$, positive before it and negative after it. That is the maximum.

Without a derivative: With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{x}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I/I_\mathrm{SC}}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{P_\mathrm{SC}\,x(1-x)}$. This parabola has the zeros 0 and 1, so its maximum $\frac14$ lies at $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{x}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12}$.

As a mechanism: A current increase $\mathrm{d} I$ brings $U_\mathrm{q}\mathrm{d} I$ out of the source, and the losses grow by $2R_\mathrm{i}I\,\mathrm{d} I$. At $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{SC}/2}$, the loss eats up the gain: 9 V against $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{2\cdot2\,\Omega\cdot2.25\,\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{9}$ V.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 7.1 (Power and efficiency)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\eta}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1-x,\qquad\frac{P_\mathrm{L}}{P_\mathrm{SC}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{x\,\eta}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{x(1-x).}$$

karten.v: How can “The steps leading to (7.3)” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{P_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q}^2}{R_\mathrm{tot}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q}^2\,(2R_\mathrm{q}+R)}{2R_\mathrm{q}(R_\mathrm{q}+R)},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\eta}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{P_\mathrm{L}}{P_\mathrm{q}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac12\,\frac{R}{2R_\mathrm{q}+R}<\frac12\quad\text{for }R<\infty.}$$
karten.s0: With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{q}R/(R_\mathrm{q}+R)}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R\parallel R_\mathrm{L}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R^2R_\mathrm{q}/(R^2+2R_\mathrm{q}R)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R\,R_\mathrm{q}/(R+2R_\mathrm{q})}$.

You solve graphically or by iteration, that is, by repeated substitution: estimate $U_\mathrm D$, calculate $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(U_0-U_\mathrm D)/R}$, then $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_T\ln(I/I_\mathrm S+1)}$, and repeat.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 6.2 (Operating point of the diode)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_0-U_\mathrm D}{R}\qquad\text{and}\qquad I}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm S\bigl(\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm D/U_T}-1\bigr).}$$
Ideal diode: a short circuit when conducting, an open circuit when blocking.

karten.v: What does “Diode with forward voltage” mean?
karten.r: Diode with forward voltage: a voltage source $U_\mathrm F$ when conducting, an open circuit when blocking.
$U_\mathrm F$ is called the forward voltage, also the forward drop.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 7.1 (Two diode models)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm D>0\ \Rightarrow\ U_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0,\qquad U_\mathrm D<0\ \Rightarrow\ I_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm D>0\ \Rightarrow\ U_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm F,\qquad U_\mathrm D<U_\mathrm F\ \Rightarrow\ I_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0.}$$
$r$ is called the differential resistance; at 1 mA it is 25.85 $\Omega$.
Lowercase letters are the deviations from the OP, the small signal.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{r}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{\mathrm{d} U_\mathrm D}{\mathrm{d} I}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_T}{I+I_\mathrm S}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_T}{I},\qquad u_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{r\,i.}$$

karten.v: How can “Slope of the characteristic curve” be derived?
karten.z:
At the OP with the direct current $I$, for small changes $u_\mathrm D$ and $i$,

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{r}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{\mathrm{d} U_\mathrm D}{\mathrm{d} I}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_T}{I+I_\mathrm S}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_T}{I},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{r\,i.}$$
(8.1)
karten.s0: Differentiating (4.1): $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathrm{d} I/\mathrm{d} U_\mathrm D}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(I_\mathrm S/U_T)\,\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm D/U_T}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(I+I_\mathrm S)/U_T}$.
s: The reciprocal is $r$.
The exponential function reproduces itself under differentiation, which is why only $I$ appears in the result, and $I_\mathrm S$ drops out in the forward direction.
Two diodes with different $I_\mathrm S$ have the same $r$ at the same current.

karten.r: The bridge rectifier (Graetz circuit) consists of four diodes in a diamond (Fig. 11).
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{u_\mathrm a}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\begin{cases}|u_\mathrm e|-2U_\mathrm F&|u_\mathrm e|>2U_\mathrm F\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}}$$

karten.v: How can “Voltage after $k$ cycles for $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{C_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{C_2}$” be derived?
karten.s0: In the first step, $C_2$ also charges to $U_\mathrm e$ through both diodes.
s: In the pump step, $C_1$ with $2U_\mathrm e$ and $C_2$ with $U_\mathrm a$ are connected.
Charge is conserved, and equal capacitors end at the mean value: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm a'}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(2U_\mathrm e+U_\mathrm a)/2}$.
The distance to the final value $2U_\mathrm e$ halves per cycle: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm a(k)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{2U_\mathrm e-U_\mathrm e\,2^{-k}}$.

karten.r: The classic representative is the bipolar transistor, a semiconductor component made of three layers with three terminals.
In n-doped silicon, electrons are free to move; in p-doped silicon, holes are: missing electrons that move like positive charges.
An npn transistor consists of three regions of the same semiconductor: n-doped emitter, p-doped base, n-doped collector (Fig. 1).

karten.v: What does “BE diode, CB diode” mean?
karten.r: The base lies between them and is very narrow, around 1 µ m. This creates two pn junctions that share the base: the BE diode and the CB diode.
Swapping n and p gives the pnp transistor (Stage 4).
In the circuit symbol, the symbol in the schematic, the emitter is the terminal with the arrow.
$I_\mathrm{C}$ is the collector current, from microamperes to amperes depending on the type.

karten.v: What does “base current, emitter current” mean?
karten.r: $I_\mathrm{B}$ is the much smaller base current, $I_\mathrm{E}$ the emitter current.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 1.1 (Currents and voltages at the npn transistor)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{E}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{B}+I_\mathrm{C},\qquad U_\mathrm{CE}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{CB}+U_\mathrm{BE}.}$$

karten.v: How can “How many quantities are free” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{E}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{B}+I_\mathrm{C},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{CE}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{CB}+U_\mathrm{BE}.}$$
(1.1)
karten.s0:
A component with $n$ terminals has $n$ currents. It stores no charge, so the node rule (Chapter 2) removes one current. It has $n$ potentials, but only differences count, so $n-1$ voltages remain. The diode ($\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{n}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{2}$) has one voltage, one current and one curve. The transistor ($\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{n}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{3}$) has two voltages and two currents. Its interior links them through two equations,

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{f(U_\mathrm{BE},U_\mathrm{CE}),}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{g(U_\mathrm{BE},U_\mathrm{CE}).}$$
s: So it is a two-port (Chapter 6) whose two ports share the emitter.

karten.r: Electrons from the emitter enter the base. This introduction is called injection.
The base is much narrower than the diffusion length, the mean distance until recombination, several tens of µ m. That is why almost all of them get through.
$I_\mathrm{C}$ is also called the transfer current, because it is transferred through the base.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 2.1 (Currents in normal operation)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{S}\,\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BE}/U_T},\qquad I_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{C}}{B},\qquad I_\mathrm{E}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\Bigl(1+\frac1B\Bigr)I_\mathrm{C}.}$$

karten.v: How can “Why $I_\mathrm{B}$ is proportional to $I_\mathrm{C}$” be derived?
karten.z:
If the BE diode conducts with $U_\mathrm{BE}\gg U_T$ and the collector lies above the base, then

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{S}\,\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BE}/U_T},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{C}}{B},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{E}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\Bigl(1+\frac1B\Bigr)I_\mathrm{C}.}$$
(2.1)
karten.s0: Electrons and holes cross the same barrier.
s: The electron density at the emitter edge of the base and the hole density at the base edge of the emitter both grow with $\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BE}/U_T}$.
The collector current is proportional to the first density, as is the recombination in the base, and the hole current is proportional to the second.
All parts carry the same factor, so their ratio $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{B}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{C}/I_\mathrm{B}}$ does not depend on $U_\mathrm{BE}$.

karten.r: Several parallel slices give a family of curves.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 3.1 (The model surface)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\underbrace{I_\mathrm{S}\,\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BE}/U_T}}_{\text{injection}}\cdot\underbrace{\bigl(1-\mathrm{e}^{-U_\mathrm{CE}/U_T}\bigr)}_{\text{collection}}\cdot\underbrace{\Bigl(1+\frac{U_\mathrm{CE}-6\,\mathrm{V}}{80\,\mathrm{V}}\Bigr)}_{\text{small slope}},\qquad I_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{S}}{B}\,\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BE}/U_T}.}$$

karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\underbrace{I_\mathrm{S}\,\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BE}/U_T}}_{\text{injection}}\cdot\underbrace{\bigl(1-\mathrm{e}^{-U_\mathrm{CE}/U_T}\bigr)}_{\text{collection}}\cdot\underbrace{\Bigl(1+\frac{U_\mathrm{CE}-6\,\mathrm{V}}{80\,\mathrm{V}}\Bigr)}_{\text{small slope}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{S}}{B}\,\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BE}/U_T}.}$$
(3.1)
karten.s0: The electron current through the base is proportional to the density gradient between its two edges.
s: Each edge follows the voltage at its boundary: $\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BE}/U_T}$ at the emitter, $\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BC}/U_T}$ at the collector, with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{BC}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-U_\mathrm{CB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{BE}-U_\mathrm{CE}}$ from (1.1).

So $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C}\sim\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BE}/U_T}-\mathrm{e}^{(U_\mathrm{BE}-U_\mathrm{CE})/U_T}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{BE}/U_T}(1-\mathrm{e}^{-U_\mathrm{CE}/U_T})}$.
The exponential function in $U_\mathrm{BE}$ and the edge in $U_\mathrm{CE}$ are two sides of one difference.

karten.r: If the BE diode blocks, no electron starts and nothing flows. This is the cut-off region.

karten.v: What does “threshold voltage, saturation voltage” mean?
karten.r: With the threshold voltage $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{BE,on}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0.6}$ V and the saturation voltage $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{CE,sat}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0.2}$ V.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 4.1 (Operating regions of the npn transistor)”?
karten.r: $$\begin{aligned} \text{Cut-off region:}\quad & U_\mathrm{BE}<U_\mathrm{BE,on}\;\Rightarrow\; I_\mathrm{B}=I_\mathrm{C}=0,\\ \text{active region:}\quad & U_\mathrm{BE}=U_\mathrm{BE,on},\ I_\mathrm{B}>0,\quad I_\mathrm{C}=B\,I_\mathrm{B},\quad U_\mathrm{CE}\ge U_\mathrm{CE,sat},\\ \text{saturation region:}\quad & U_\mathrm{BE}=U_\mathrm{BE,on},\ I_\mathrm{B}>0,\quad U_\mathrm{CE}=U_\mathrm{CE,sat},\quad I_\mathrm{C}\le B\,I_\mathrm{B}. \end{aligned}$$
$U_\mathrm{CC}$ is the supply voltage, $U_\mathrm{in}$ the input voltage against ground.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 5.1 (Operating point of the circuit with base and collector resistor)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{in}-U_\mathrm{BE,on}}{R_\mathrm{B}}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{B\,I_\mathrm{B},\qquad U_\mathrm{CE}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{CC}-B\,I_\mathrm{B}R_\mathrm{C}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{CE}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{CE,sat},\qquad I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{CC}-U_\mathrm{CE,sat}}{R_\mathrm{C}}<B\,I_\mathrm{B}.}$$
The smallest logic circuit is the inverter: the same circuit as in Fig. 6, with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{out}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{CE}}$ as the output.
As logic levels, a low voltage counts as 0 and a high one as 1.
Above the power hyperbola $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{P_\mathrm{max}/U_\mathrm{CE}}$ the component becomes too hot.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 6.1 (Characteristic of the inverter)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{out}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{ \begin{cases} U_\mathrm{CC} & U_\mathrm{in}<U_\mathrm{BE},\\[2pt] U_\mathrm{CC}-B\,R_\mathrm{C}\dfrac{U_\mathrm{in}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{R_\mathrm{B}} & U_\mathrm{BE}\le U_\mathrm{in}\le U_\mathrm{in,sat},\\[6pt] U_\mathrm{CE,sat} & U_\mathrm{in}>U_\mathrm{in,sat}, \end{cases}}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{in,sat}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{(U_\mathrm{CC}-U_\mathrm{CE,sat})\,R_\mathrm{B}}{B\,R_\mathrm{C}}+U_\mathrm{BE}.}$$
The effect weakens its cause: this is negative feedback, here current feedback, because the current through $R_\mathrm{E}$ produces the opposing voltage.

If $I_\mathrm{C}$ rises, $U_\mathrm{CE}$ falls, and with it $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(U_\mathrm{CE}-U_\mathrm{BE})/R_\mathrm{B}}$ falls. This is voltage feedback.

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 7.1 (Operating point with negative feedback)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{CC}\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2},\quad I_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{(1+B)R_\mathrm{E}+R_\mathrm{i}},\quad I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{R_\mathrm{E}\bigl(1+\frac1B\bigr)+\frac{R_\mathrm{i}}{B}}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{CC}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{R_\mathrm{C}\bigl(1+\frac1B\bigr)+\frac{R_\mathrm{B}}{B}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{CC}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{R_\mathrm{C}+\frac{R_\mathrm{B}}{B}},\qquad\text{for } R_\mathrm{C}\gg\frac{R_\mathrm{B}}{B}:\ I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{CC}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{R_\mathrm{C}}.}$$

karten.v: How can “The formulas from the meshes” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{CC}\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2},\quad I_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{(1+B)R_\mathrm{E}+R_\mathrm{i}},\quad I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{q}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{R_\mathrm{E}\bigl(1+\frac1B\bigr)+\frac{R_\mathrm{i}}{B}}.}$$
(7.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{CC}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{R_\mathrm{C}\bigl(1+\frac1B\bigr)+\frac{R_\mathrm{B}}{B}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{CC}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{R_\mathrm{C}+\frac{R_\mathrm{B}}{B}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\text{for } R_\mathrm{C}\gg\frac{R_\mathrm{B}}{B}:\ I_\mathrm{C}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{CC}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{R_\mathrm{C}}.}$$
(7.2)
karten.s0:
The divider becomes the source $U_\mathrm{q}$ with $R_\mathrm{i}$ in series. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{E}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(1+B)I_\mathrm{B}}$, the mesh through base and emitter reads

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{q}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{B}R_\mathrm{i}+U_\mathrm{BE}+I_\mathrm{B}(1+B)R_\mathrm{E}.}$$
s:
Solving for $I_\mathrm{B}$ and multiplying by $B$ gives (7.1). With voltage feedback, the current $I_\mathrm{C}+I_\mathrm{B}$ flows through $R_\mathrm{C}$, and only $I_\mathrm{B}$ through $R_\mathrm{B}$. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{C}/B}$, the mesh reads

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{CC}-U_\mathrm{BE}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\Bigl(\frac{I_\mathrm{C}}{B}+I_\mathrm{C}\Bigr)R_\mathrm{C}+\frac{I_\mathrm{C}}{B}R_\mathrm{B}.}$$
Solving for $I_\mathrm{C}$ gives (7.2).

karten.r: In the current mirror (Fig. 9, left), T1 is connected as a diode: base and collector are joined.
$I_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference current.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{ref}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{CC}-U_\mathrm{BE}}{R_\mathrm{ref}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_\mathrm{C1}+I_\mathrm{B1}+I_\mathrm{B2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(B+2)I_\mathrm{B2},\qquad I_\mathrm{C2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{B\,I_\mathrm{B2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{ref}}{1+\frac2B}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{ I_\mathrm{ref}.}$$

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 8.2 (Voltage regulator with Zener diode)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{Z}-U_\mathrm{BE}.}$$
The small letters with small indices are called small-signal quantities.
The symbol $\partial$ stands for the partial derivative: the derivative with respect to one variable while the others are held fixed, that is, the slope of a slice.
The transconductance $S$ in A/V is the slope of the control characteristic, $r_\mathrm{BE}$ the input resistance, the slope of the input characteristic read inversely.
The Early voltage $U_\mathrm{Early}$ typically lies between 50 V and 200 V; for T it is 74 V. Mechanism: more $U_\mathrm{CB}$ widens the space-charge region into the base.
The extended equivalent circuit contains the DC components.
Leaving out the DC components leaves the small-signal equivalent circuit.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 9.1 (Small-signal quantities at the operating point)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{S}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{\partial I_\mathrm{C}}{\partial U_\mathrm{BE}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{C}}{U_T},\qquad r_\mathrm{BE}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{\partial U_\mathrm{BE}}{\partial I_\mathrm{B}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_T}{I_\mathrm{B}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{B}{S},\qquad G_\mathrm{CE}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac1{r_\mathrm{CE}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{\partial I_\mathrm{C}}{\partial U_\mathrm{CE}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_\mathrm{C}}{U_\mathrm{Early}+U_\mathrm{CE}}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{i_\mathrm{b}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{u_\mathrm{be}}{r_\mathrm{BE}},\qquad i_\mathrm{c}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{S\,u_\mathrm{be}+\frac{u_\mathrm{ce}}{r_\mathrm{CE}}.}$$

(9.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{i_\mathrm{b}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{u_\mathrm{be}}{r_\mathrm{BE}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{i_\mathrm{c}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{S\,u_\mathrm{be}+\frac{u_\mathrm{ce}}{r_\mathrm{CE}}.}$$

An operational amplifier, op amp for short, is an integrated amplifier made of a few dozen transistors.
That is why noise is described by the noise voltage density $|u_\mathrm{r}(f)|^2$: the contribution of each frequency strip 1 Hz wide to the square of the rms value.
The signal-to-noise ratio is the ratio of the powers, written in decibels (dB).
Constant density is called white noise, after white light made of all colors.
That is a limit of the model: real densities fall off at very high frequencies, and every circuit has a finite bandwidth $\Delta f$, the frequency range it passes.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{I_0}{1+\mathrm{e}^{U_\mathrm{D}/U_T}},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{C}\,(I_\mathrm{C2}-I_\mathrm{C1}).}$$
(2.1)

Together with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_\mathrm{C1}+I_\mathrm{C2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{I_0}$ this gives (2.1).
For small changes: the sum is fixed, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\Delta I_\mathrm{C1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\Delta I_\mathrm{C2}}$.
Both are $S$ times the change in their own $U_\mathrm{BE}$, so the changes are equal and opposite.
Their difference is $U_\mathrm{D}$, so each junction carries $\pm U_\mathrm{D}/2$.

Thus $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\Delta I_\mathrm{C2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{S\,U_\mathrm{D}/2}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{2R_\mathrm{C}\,\Delta I_\mathrm{C2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{S\,R_\mathrm{C}\,U_\mathrm{D}}$.

The ideal op amp has $r_\mathrm{e}\to\infty$ (no input current), $A\to\infty$ at all frequencies, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{r_\mathrm{a}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$ (the output current adjusts itself so that all node and mesh equations are satisfied) and no noise.

karten.v: What is the formula “Definition 3.1 (Model of the op amp)”?
karten.r: $$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{D}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varphi_+-\varphi_-,\qquad U_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\begin{cases}U_\mathrm{A,max}&\text{for }A\,U_\mathrm{D}\ge U_\mathrm{A,max},\\A\,U_\mathrm{D}&\text{in between},\\U_\mathrm{A,min}&\text{for }A\,U_\mathrm{D}\le U_\mathrm{A,min}.\end{cases}}$$
Feedback means that part of the output quantity gets back to the input.
In the non-inverting amplifier, $U_\mathrm{E}$ is at the plus input (Fig. 6).

karten.v: What is the formula “Theorem 4.1 (Amplifier with negative feedback)”?
karten.r:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{D}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{E}}{1+A\beta},\qquad G}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{A}}{U_\mathrm{E}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{A}{1+A\beta}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac1\beta\cdot\frac{1}{1+\dfrac1{A\beta}}.}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{\Delta G}{G}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{1+A\beta}\cdot\frac{\Delta A}{A}.}$$

karten.v: The gain is the ______ of the fed-back fraction. Limiting cases: $A\to\infty$ gives $U_\mathrm{D}\to0$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1/\beta}$. $\beta\to0$ gives $G\to A$; without feedback, the open loop remains.
karten.r: The gain is the reciprocal of the fed-back fraction. Limiting cases: $A\to\infty$ gives $U_\mathrm{D}\to0$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1/\beta}$. $\beta\to0$ gives $G\to A$; without feedback, the open loop remains.

karten.v: How can “The loop in equilibrium and in motion” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{D}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{E}}{1+A\beta},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{G}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{A}}{U_\mathrm{E}}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{A}{1+A\beta}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac1\beta\cdot\frac{1}{1+\dfrac1{A\beta}}.}$$
(4.1)
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{\Delta G}{G}}\textcolor{#15633a}{\approx}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{1}{1+A\beta}\cdot\frac{\Delta A}{A}.}$$
(4.2)
karten.s0: Equilibrium: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A\,U_\mathrm{D}}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{D}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{E}-\beta\,U_\mathrm{A}}$. Substituting gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{D}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{E}-A\beta\,U_\mathrm{D}}$, and from this (4.1). Differentiating $G$ with respect to $A$ gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathrm{d} G/\mathrm{d} A}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{1/(1+A\beta)^2}$; dividing by $G$ yields (4.2).
s:
Motion: inside the op amp, a current proportional to $U_\mathrm{D}$ charges a capacitance. The output therefore cannot jump but runs after its target value: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau\,\mathrm{d} U_\mathrm{A}/\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A\,U_\mathrm{D}-U_\mathrm{A}}$, here with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A/(2\pi f_\mathrm{T})}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{15.9}$ ms. This is the equation of the RC circuit from Chapter 3. With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{D}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_\mathrm{E}-\beta\,U_\mathrm{A}}$ it becomes

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau\,\frac{\mathrm{d} U_\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{d} t}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A\,U_\mathrm{E}-(1+A\beta)\,U_\mathrm{A}.}$$

The factor in front of $U_\mathrm{A}$ is negative, so every deviation decays: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{A}(t)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{G\,U_\mathrm{E}\,(1-\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_G})}$ with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau_G}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\tau/(1+A\beta)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0.80}$ µ s. The loop is 20001 times faster than the op amp alone.

karten.r: In the inverting amplifier, the plus input is at ground, $U_\mathrm{E}$ arrives at the minus input through $R_1$, and $R_2$ leads back from the output (Fig. 7).

karten.v: How can “Finite $A$ in the inverting amplifier” be derived?
karten.z:
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\frac{U_\mathrm{E}}{R_1}+\frac{U_\mathrm{A}}{R_2}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0\quad\Rightarrow\quad U_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\frac{R_2}{R_1}\,U_\mathrm{E},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{in}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_\mathrm{E}}{I_1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_1.}$$
karten.s0: Superposition at the divider of $R_1$ and $R_2$ gives $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi_-}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(R_2\,U_\mathrm{E}+R_1\,U_\mathrm{A})/(R_1+R_2)}$.
s: With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\varphi_+}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0}$, $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{D}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-\varphi_-}$, so $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-A\,\varphi_-}$.

Solving: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{A}(1+A\beta)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-A\,(1-\beta)\,U_\mathrm{E}}$ with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{1-\beta}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_2/(R_1+R_2)}$.
Because $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{A(1-\beta)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A\beta\cdot R_2/R_1}$, the formula follows.
The loop sees $U_\mathrm{E}$ as a fixed value, so $\beta$ is the same divider as in Stage 4.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{in}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{U_1}{I_1}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-R_2.}$$
(8.2)

The rule holds only as long as the resistance $R_\mathrm{i}$ that acts at terminal 1 with respect to ground is smaller than $R_2$.
karten.s0: Through $R_2$ flows $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_2}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_2/R_2}$, and no current goes into the input, so it also flows through the lower $R$: the output is at $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_2+R\,I_2}$. The upper $R$ has the same voltage and carries the same current, from the output to terminal 1. So $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-I_2}$ and $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{R_\mathrm{in}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{U_1/I_1}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{-R_2}$.
s: There are two feedback paths here: the lower $R$ gives negative feedback, the left one positive feedback. If $U_\mathrm{A}$ changes, $\varphi_-$ changes by the fraction $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\beta_-}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_2/(R_2+R)}$ and $\varphi_+$ by $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\beta_+}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_\mathrm{i}/(R_\mathrm{i}+R)}$. Negative feedback prevails only for $\beta_->\beta_+$, that is, for $R_\mathrm{i}<R_2$.

karten.r: The circuit is called an inverting Schmitt trigger.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\text{downward at }U_\mathrm{E}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\beta\,U_\mathrm{A,max},\qquad\text{upward at }U_\mathrm{E}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\beta\,U_\mathrm{A,min}.}$$

karten.v: How can “The same equation, a different sign” be derived?
karten.z:
With $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\beta}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{R_1/(R_1+R_2)}$ the output flips

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\text{downward at }U_\mathrm{E}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\beta\,U_\mathrm{A,max},}$$
$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\text{upward at }U_\mathrm{E}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\beta\,U_\mathrm{A,min}.}$$
(9.1)

The width of the hysteresis is $\beta\,(U_\mathrm{A,max}-U_\mathrm{A,min})$. Between the thresholds both states are possible.
karten.s0: With the sluggishness from Stage 4, now $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau\,\mathrm{d} U_\mathrm{A}/\mathrm{d} t}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A(\beta\,U_\mathrm{A}-U_\mathrm{E})-U_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{(A\beta-1)\,U_\mathrm{A}-A\,U_\mathrm{E}}$.
s: The factor in front of $U_\mathrm{A}$ is now positive.

A deviation from equilibrium grows like $\mathrm{e}^{+t/\tau_\mathrm{M}}$ with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\tau_\mathrm{M}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\tau/(A\beta-1)}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{0.80}$ µ s, the same size as in Stage 4.
In this way a disturbance of 1 µ V becomes the 11 V in 13 µ s. An unlimited supply would give an unlimited rise; the circuit would be unstable.
Only saturation stops it.

karten.r: The common-mode rejection CMRR (common mode rejection ratio) compares the gain of the difference with that of the common mode.
Otherwise the op amp is overdriven: $U_\mathrm{A}$ is at its limit, $U_\mathrm{D}\ne0$, and you calculate the network with this fixed $U_\mathrm{A}$.

$$\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{\mathrm{CMRR}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\frac{A}{A_\mathrm{cm}},\qquad \mathrm{CMRR}_\mathrm{dB}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{20\lg\frac{A}{A_\mathrm{cm}}.}$$

Inside sits a differential amplifier, a circuit that responds only to the difference between two voltages: $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{A}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{A\,U_\mathrm{D}}$ with $\textcolor{#1b7f4a}{U_\mathrm{D}}\textcolor{#15633a}{=}\textcolor{#c2410c}{\varphi_+-\varphi_-}$.
